lead: A lathe is the oldest and most common machine tool. It grips the workpiece in a chuck and spins it, while a single-point tool is pushed into the rotating surface. Because the work turns and the tool only translates, every cut sweeps a circle, so the result is a surface of revolution: a cylinder, a shoulder, a taper or a screw thread. Shafts, bushes, pulleys, bolts and axle pins are all born on a lathe. Turned parts are the starting point for most other machining, which is why the lathe is the first machine tool in any workshop.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for cutting action, 5.3 for tool geometry, and 5.5 for tool life, which sets the cutting speed you may use.

sections.h3: Parts that hold the work and move the tool

blocks.text: The bed is a rigid cast-iron base with machined guideways on top. Every sliding member rides these ways, so the bed decides the accuracy of the whole machine.

The headstock is fixed at the left end. It carries the spindle, driven by belts or gears from the motor, and the chuck or faceplate that grips the work. The tailstock slides on the ways at the right end; its quill holds a centre to support the free end of a long bar, or a drill for making holes.

The carriage slides along the bed between the two ends. On it sit the cross-slide, which moves the tool at right angles to the axis, the compound rest, which can be swivelled to any angle for short tapers, and the tool post, which clamps the tool.

items: Feed rod: drives the carriage and cross-slide for ordinary turning and facing.
Lead screw: a precision screw that moves the carriage in step with the spindle, giving the fixed ratio needed for thread cutting.
Two motions: the cutting motion is the rotation of the work and sets the cutting speed; the feed motion is the travel of the tool and sets the chip thickness.

blocks.text: Never use the lead screw for plain turning. The carriage travel for turning is fast and continuous, and it wears a screw that must stay accurate for threads.

Speed lathe: the simplest form. Headstock, tailstock and a hand-operated tool rest, with no carriage and no power feed. Spindle speeds are high, and it is used for wood turning, polishing and metal spinning.
Bench lathe: a small lathe mounted on a bench for fine work on small parts.

Engine lathe: the general-purpose machine, also called a centre lathe. It has a sliding carriage, a powered feed rod, a lead screw, a compound rest and back gears that give a wide range of spindle speeds. This is the default lathe of a workshop.
Toolroom lathe: an engine lathe built to closer tolerances, with a wider speed range and more accessories. It makes jigs, fixtures and gauges, where the size tolerance is tight.

Capstan and turret lathe: the tailstock is replaced by a hexagonal turret that indexes to bring six preset tools into position in turn. The carriage carries a four-way tool post, and adjustable stops set the travel of each slide. The operator does not measure every part; the machine repeats a fixed sequence, so unskilled labour can hold the size and the cycle time is short. It suits batch production, typically hundreds to a few thousand identical parts per batch, before the setup cost forces a move to an automatic lathe.

Automatic lathe: cams, or a control system, sequence every motion with no operator. Single-spindle and multi-spindle versions make small parts in very large numbers. CNC lathes replace cams and handwheels with servo axes driven by a part program; see Unit 6, CNC and Non-Traditional Machining.

sections.h3: Operations and the numbers behind them

blocks.text: Turning reduces the diameter over a length: the tool feeds along the axis. Facing produces a flat end: the tool feeds radially inward. Chamfering cuts a sloped edge on a corner. Grooving cuts a narrow recess, for example a circlip groove. Parting, or cutting off, feeds a thin tool radially to the centre to separate the finished part.

Knurling presses a patterned roller into the surface for grip; it is a forming operation, not a cutting one. Drilling is done from the tailstock, and boring enlarges and trues an existing hole with a single-point tool. Threading uses the lead screw so that one spindle revolution advances the tool by exactly the pitch. Taper turning is done by swivelling the compound rest, by setting over the tailstock, or with a taper turning attachment.

blocks.where: N is spindle speed in rev/min; v is cutting speed in m/min; D is the workpiece diameter in mm; 1000 converts metres to millimetres.

blocks.text: fₘ = f N    and    T = L / (f N)
blocks.where: f is feed in mm/rev; fₘ is feed rate in mm/min; N is spindle speed in rev/min; T is machining time in min; L is tool travel along the feed direction in mm, including approach and overtravel.
MRR is the material removal rate in mm³/min; v is cutting speed in m/min; f is feed in mm/rev; d is depth of cut in mm, measured radially.

blocks.text: Depth of cut is measured from the surface to the tool nose, that is, radially. The tool removes a layer of thickness d from the radius (one side only), so the radius falls by d and the diameter, being twice the radius, falls by 2d in one pass.

figure.caption: The headstock turns the work on its axis while the tailstock supports the far end. The carriage rides the bed, the cross-slide sets depth, and the two shafts decide whether the carriage is driven for turning or locked to the spindle for threading.

examples.question: A mild steel bar of 50 mm diameter is to be turned down to 44 mm over a length of 150 mm. Cutting speed is 30 m/min, feed is 0.2 mm/rev and the depth of cut is 2 mm per pass. Find the spindle speed, the feed rate, the machining time per pass, the material removal rate and the number of passes needed. State the total turning time.
steps: Data: D₁ = 50 mm, D₂ = 44 mm, L = 150 mm, v = 30 m/min, f = 0.2 mm/rev, d = 2 mm per pass.
Spindle speed: N = 1000 v / (π D₁) = (1000 × 30) / (π × 50) = 30 000 / 157.08 = 190.99 rev/min, so about 191 rpm.
Feed rate: fₘ = f N = 0.2 × 190.99 = 38.2 mm/min.
Time per pass: T = L / (f N) = 150 / 38.2 = 3.93 min.
Material removal rate: MRR = 1000 v f d = 1000 × 30 × 0.2 × 2 = 12 000 mm³/min.

Stock to remove on radius: (D₁ − D₂)/2 = (50 − 44)/2 = 3 mm. Passes = 3 / 2 = 1.5, so 2 passes; the first takes 2 mm of radius (diameter 50 → 46 mm) and the second takes the remaining 1 mm (diameter 46 → 44 mm).
examples.answer: N ≈ 191 rpm, feed rate ≈ 38.2 mm/min, time ≈ 3.93 min per pass, MRR = 12 000 mm³/min, 2 passes, total turning time ≈ 7.85 min.
examples.check:
import math
D1, D2, L, v, f, d = 50.0, 44.0, 150.0, 30.0, 0.2, 2.0
N = 1000*v/(math.pi*D1)
feed_rate = f*N
T = L/feed_rate
mrr = 1000*v*f*d
passes = math.ceil((D1-D2)/2/d)
print(round(N,2))
print(round(feed_rate,2))
print(round(T,2))
print(round(mrr,1))
print(passes)
print(round(passes*T,2))

traps: Depth of cut is radial, so the diameter drops by 2d per pass. Students who count the diameter reduction per pass as d instead of 2d get twice the number of passes (3 instead of 1.5). The correct pass count is (D₁ − D₂)/(2d).

Feed is in mm/rev and feed rate is in mm/min. Dividing the length by f instead of by f N gives an answer larger by a factor of N (750 min instead of 3.93 min), because feed per revolution is not a speed.
The lead screw is for threading only; ordinary turning and facing use the feed rod. An examiner may ask why the two are separate.
For facing, the tool travel L is the radial distance from the outer edge to the centre, not the length of the job.
A turret lathe has no tailstock. Its hex turret does the work of the tailstock and also carries several cutting tools.

quiz.q: Name the lathe part that rotates the workpiece and the part that supports its free end.
quiz.a: The headstock rotates the work through the spindle and chuck; the tailstock supports the free end with a centre.

quiz.q: Which element moves the carriage during thread cutting, and why is it not used for plain turning?
quiz.a: The lead screw, because it is geared to the spindle and gives one pitch of carriage travel per revolution. Using it for turning wears a screw that must stay accurate for threads.

quiz.q: Why does the workpiece diameter fall by twice the depth of cut in one pass?
quiz.a: The tool is set inwards by d from the surface, so it removes d from the radius. The radius drops by d on one side of the axis, and the diameter, being twice the radius, drops by 2d.

quiz.q: A 60 mm diameter bar is turned at a cutting speed of 25 m/min with a feed of 0.25 mm/rev. Find the spindle speed and the feed rate.
A shaft is turned over 200 mm at 400 rpm with a feed of 0.3 mm/rev. Find the machining time for one pass.
quiz.a: Feed rate = 0.3 × 400 = 120 mm/min. Time = L / (f N) = 200 / 120 = 1.67 min.

quiz.q: A batch of 5 000 identical pins must be turned. Explain why a turret lathe beats an engine lathe, and name two ways of turning a taper on a lathe.
quiz.a: On a turret lathe six tools sit preset on the indexing turret and four on the square post, and stops fix each travel. The operator repeats a sequence without measuring, so setup is paid once and cycle time, idle time and skill demand all fall. Tapers: swivel the compound rest for short steep tapers, set over the tailstock for long shallow tapers on a shaft, or use a taper turning attachment.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern turning shops run CNC lathes with live tooling, where a driven tool in the turret also mills flats and drills off-centre holes, so one machine finishes a part that once needed three. Hard turning uses cubic boron nitride tools to finish hardened shafts without grinding. Search next for live tooling, subspindle lathes, and bar feeders for unattended production.
